recipe: Shrink hot types: over 128 bytes triggers memcpy. Box the rare oversized enum variant. u32 indices, not usize. Boxed slice or ThinVec over Vec. Pin it with assert_eq_size!.
trigger_condition: Do hot types exceed 128 bytes?

recipe: Do not hand-reorder fields to kill padding: rustc already sorts struct and enum fields. Manual layout only matters under #[repr(C)]. Inspect with -Zprint-type-sizes.
trigger_condition: Does the code manually reorder fields to reduce padding?

recipe: Per-thread counters sharing a cache line cause false sharing and kill throughput. Wrap each in crossbeam_utils::CachePadded, which pads and aligns to 128 bytes on x86-64 and aarch64 (not 64) and to target-specific sizes elsewhere.
trigger_condition: Do per-thread counters share a cache line?
_original_recipe: Per-thread counters sharing a cache line kill throughput. Wrap each in crossbeam CachePadded: 128 bytes on x86-64/aarch64, not 64. Padding only; inner T keeps the same address.
_review_reason: 'inner T keeps the same address' is unsupported and confusing; sizes vary by target

recipe: Vec::with_capacity when the size is known: four allocations collapse to one. Hoist the buffer out of the loop and clear() it. clone_from reuses the destination allocation.
trigger_condition: Does the code allocate a Vec of known size repeatedly?

recipe: Small collection inside a hot type: SmallVec<[T; N]> stays inline. Mixed borrowed/owned: Cow, not to_string(). format! allocates, so skip it for plain literals.
trigger_condition: Does the hot type contain a small fixed-size collection?

recipe: Many nodes with one shared lifetime: arena-allocate once, as rustc does with its 'tcx arena, and intern so equality is a pointer compare instead of a deep structural walk.
source_name: rustc dev guide: Memory management in rustc
trigger_condition: Do many nodes share one lifetime?

recipe: Allocation-heavy workload: try jemalloc or mimalloc before micro-optimizing call sites. Costs binary size and build time, and the win is workload-dependent. Measure it.
Bounds checks in the hot loop: iterate instead of indexing, bind the slice before the loop, assert the index range up front. get_unchecked last, and only with a benchmark.
trigger_condition: Does the hot loop index a sequence with bounds checks?

recipe: Bounds checks come out without unsafe: zip parallel slices, slice both to one common length first, index through iterators. Verify in the asm with cargo-show-asm.
trigger_condition: Does the code iterate over two slices in parallel?

recipe: chunks_exact plus remainder beats chunks. filter_map beats filter().map(). chain can be slower than a single iterator. iter().copied() sometimes unlocks better codegen for small Copy types.
trigger_condition: Does the existing code use Rust iterators?

recipe: Do not collect just to re-iterate: return impl Iterator<Item=T>. extend into an existing Vec instead of collecting a fresh one. Implement size_hint on custom iterators.
trigger_condition: Does the code collect into a Vec only to iterate it?

recipe: Default HashMap SipHash resists HashDoS but is slow, especially on integer keys. If profiling shows hashing is hot and untrusted input cannot reach the keys, switch to rustc-hash's FxHashMap (rustc saw 4-84% slowdowns going back to the default). Try several hashers and measure.
trigger_condition: Does untrusted input reach the HashMap keys?
_original_recipe: HashMap's SipHash is DoS-resistant and slow on integer keys. Swap rustc-hash FxHashMap when hashing shows in the profile and untrusted input cannot reach it. Sometimes 1-4% slower; measure.
_review_reason: misattributed number: the 1-4% slowdown in the perf book was fxhash->ahash, not FxHash vs SipHash; going back to the default hasher cost rustc 4-84%

recipe: #[inline] is a hint, #[inline(always)] nearly a command; cross-crate inlining needs the attribute but duplicates IR. Effects are unpredictable and sometimes negative. Benchmark each one.
trigger_condition: Does the code use #[inline] attributes?

recipe: vec![0; n] for zero-fill. swap_remove (O(1)) over remove when order is free. retain for bulk deletes. unwrap_or_else/ok_or_else when the fallback is expensive to build.
Before profiling: release build, lto = "thin" or "fat", codegen-units = 1, panic = "abort". -C target-cpu=native buys AVX at the cost of portability. PGO adds roughly ten percent.
C-GENERIC: take generics, not concrete types; AsRef<str> over &String. C-CALLER-CONTROL: the caller decides where data is copied and placed. Collections implement FromIterator and Extend.
C-ITER: collections expose iter / iter_mut / into_iter. C-ITER-TY: name the iterator type after the method producing it. Conversions go through From, AsRef, AsMut.
Split hot fields from cold ones so the cache line carries only what the loop reads. Drepper measures up to 5x. Run pahole and close the holes.
source_name: Drepper, What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory, Part 5

recipe: Put the most likely critical member first in the struct, and read members in declaration order, so the critical word arrives first out of the cache line.
source_name: Drepper, What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory, Part 5
trigger_condition: Does the code read a struct's critical member first?

recipe: Align big arrays to the cache line: posix_memalign, or __attribute__((aligned(64))) for automatics. Unaligned access costs 20-30% on large working sets, far worse streaming out of L2.
source_name: Drepper, What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory, Part 5
trigger_condition: Does the code stream through arrays larger than one cache line?

recipe: Do not hardcode 64. Query sysconf(_SC_LEVEL1_DCACHE_LINESIZE) at runtime, or getconf at build time, then derive your blocking factor from it.
source_name: Drepper, What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory, Part 5
trigger_condition: Does the code hardcode 64 as a blocking factor?

recipe: If the loop reads a[i] and b[i] together, one array of structs beats two arrays. SoA only wins when the loop touches a subset of fields. Know which case you have.
source_name: Agner Fog, Optimizing software in C++, section 10.4
license_if_known: Copyright Agner Fog; CC-BY-SA 4.0 takes effect posthumously
trigger_condition: Does the loop touch all fields of each item?

recipe: Keep hot variables local so they live on the stack and likely in L1. Avoid globals, statics, and dynamic allocation for data that is used together.
source_name: Agner Fog, Optimizing software in C++, section 10.4
license_if_known: Copyright Agner Fog; CC-BY-SA 4.0 takes effect posthumously
trigger_condition: Are hot variables allocated outside the local stack?

recipe: malloc/free in hot code costs far more than stack storage, fragments the heap, and wrecks caching. Hoist the allocation out of the loop and reuse the buffer.
source_name: Agner Fog, Optimizing software in C++, section 10.6
license_if_known: Copyright Agner Fog; CC-BY-SA 4.0 takes effect posthumously
trigger_condition: Does the hot loop allocate memory?

recipe: Many small variable-size objects, strings especially: put them all in one memory pool. A malloc per object is where the fragmentation and heap-management overhead comes from.
source_name: Agner Fog, Optimizing software in C++, section 2.8
license_if_known: Copyright Agner Fog; CC-BY-SA 4.0 takes effect posthumously
trigger_condition: Are many small variable-size objects allocated separately?

recipe: Short-lived, small, bounded variable-size array: alloca puts it on the stack (no fragmentation, free deallocation, contiguous with other stack data). Never return a pointer into it, never use it for unbounded sizes, and check your compiler's restrictions.
source_name: Agner Fog, Optimizing software in C++, section 10.6
license_if_known: Copyright Agner Fog; CC-BY-SA 4.0 takes effect posthumously
trigger_condition: Is the variable-size array short-lived?
_original_recipe: Short-lived variable-size array: alloca puts it on the stack. No fragmentation, free deallocation, contiguous with other stack data. Never return a pointer into it; check your compiler's restrictions.
_review_reason: alloca needs the bounded-size caveat (stack overflow)

recipe: Access memory sequentially: backwards is slower, random much slower. For row-major C arrays a[i][j], put the last index (j) in the innermost loop; the swapped order strides across rows and misses cache.
source_name: Agner Fog, Optimizing software in C++, section 10.9
license_if_known: Copyright Agner Fog; CC-BY-SA 4.0 takes effect posthumously
trigger_condition: Does the code access a multidimensional array?
_original_recipe: Access sequentially. Backwards is slower, random much slower. Multidimensional arrays: last index in the innermost loop. Do not swap those two loops.
_review_reason: 'Do not swap those two loops' is ambiguous

recipe: A matrix row stride that is a high power of two hits the critical stride and thrashes cache sets; transposes and tiled kernels stall. Pad the row or block the loop.
source_name: Agner Fog, Optimizing software in C++, section 10.10
license_if_known: Copyright Agner Fog; CC-BY-SA 4.0 takes effect posthumously
trigger_condition: Is the matrix row stride a high power of two?

recipe: Misprediction costs roughly 15-25 cycles; a predicted branch costs 0-2. Compute the condition early, prefer integer comparisons over float, and keep 50/50 branches out of the hot loop.
source_name: Agner Fog, Optimizing software in C++, section 7.12
license_if_known: Copyright Agner Fog; CC-BY-SA 4.0 takes effect posthumously
trigger_condition: Does the hot loop contain a branch with a 50/50 outcome?

recipe: Reach for __builtin_expect only where profiling is impossible. GCC's own manual says programmers are notoriously bad at predicting this; prefer -fprofile-arcs feedback.
trigger_condition: Is profiling impossible here?

recipe: Auto-vectorization needs: restrict pointers, no element-level branches or table lookups, trip count divisible by the vector width, arrays aligned 32 for AVX and 64 for AVX512. Read the asm.
source_name: Agner Fog, Optimizing software in C++, section 13.3
license_if_known: Copyright Agner Fog; CC-BY-SA 4.0 takes effect posthumously

recipe: restrict on non-overlapping pointer parameters lets the compiler drop the reload after every store and vectorize. It is a promise, not a hint: alias through it and behavior is undefined.
trigger_condition: Do the pointer parameters point to non-overlapping memory?

recipe: Predictable but non-sequential reads: _mm_prefetch(ptr, _MM_HINT_T0). Write-once data you will not re-read: non-temporal stores such as _mm_stream_si128, to avoid polluting the cache.
source_name: Drepper, What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory, Part 5
trigger_condition: Does the code read predictable but non-sequential data?

recipe: Hardware prefetchers cannot cross page boundaries and need a recognizable pattern. Tile loops by cache line, SM = CLS/sizeof(elem). Drepper's tiled matrix multiply ran in about 17% of the original time, under 10% once SIMD was added.
source_name: Drepper, What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory, Part 5
trigger_condition: Does the code access a large array in a predictable pattern?
_original_recipe: Hardware prefetchers cannot cross page boundaries and need a recognizable pattern. Tile loops by cache line: SM = CLS/sizeof(elem). Drepper's tiled matmul hit roughly ten percent of original time.
_review_reason: number wrong: Drepper's sub-matrix (tiled) matmul ran in 17.3% of original time; ~10% (9.47%) only after adding SIMD

recipe: Per.16, Per.18, Per.19: compact data structures, space is time, access memory predictably. Row-major traversal with the inner loop over columns; the transposed version is the classic cache-miss bug.
license_if_known: Standard C++ Foundation license (personal/internal business use)
trigger_condition: Does the code traverse a 2D array?

recipe: Per.17: declare the most used member of a time-critical struct first. Per.12 and Per.13: eliminate redundant aliases and redundant indirections; each pointer hop is another potential miss.
license_if_known: Standard C++ Foundation license (personal/internal business use)
trigger_condition: Does the hot path dereference a struct pointer?

recipe: Two atomics written by two threads in one cache line: alignas(std::hardware_destructive_interference_size). cppreference's own benchmark shows about 6x. Use hardware_constructive_interference_size to keep co-read data together.
trigger_condition: Do two threads write two atomics in one cache line?

recipe: alignas(64) on big arrays lands the start on a cache-line boundary. Objects over 16 bytes want 16-byte alignment; the compiler handles scalars. Class member padding wastes cache space.
source_name: Agner Fog, Optimizing software in C++, section 10.5
license_if_known: Copyright Agner Fog; CC-BY-SA 4.0 takes effect posthumously
trigger_condition: Does the code use large arrays of structs?

recipe: Scattered bools in hot structs waste most of the cache line you already paid for (Acton, CppCon 2014). Pack flags into bitfields or move them to a separate array, and count L2 misses per frame to judge the layout.
source_name: Mike Acton, Data-Oriented Design and C++, CppCon 2014 slides
trigger_condition: Are bools scattered in struct fields?
_original_recipe: bools scattered in structs are near-zero information density for a whole cache line. Acton: count the L2 misses per frame and fill the line you already paid for.

recipe: Per.14 and Per.15: minimize allocations and deallocations, and never allocate on a critical branch. Move the allocation out of the hot path entirely rather than making it faster.
license_if_known: Standard C++ Foundation license (personal/internal business use)
trigger_condition: Does the hot path allocate memory?

recipe: ES.71: prefer range-for when you have the choice, it cannot get the bounds wrong. ES.55: design away the need for range checking instead of optimizing the check.
source_name: C++ Core Guidelines, ES: Expressions and statements
license_if_known: Standard C++ Foundation license (personal/internal business use)
trigger_condition: Does the code iterate over a container by index?

recipe: Hoist loop-invariant member reads and branches out by hand, even obvious ones. Conservative aliasing rules force the compiler to re-read members it should already have in a register.
source_name: Mike Acton, Data-Oriented Design and C++, CppCon 2014 slides
trigger_condition: Does the loop read a member that never changes?

recipe: F.18: will-move-from parameters take X&& and std::move inside. ES.56: write std::move only to move across scopes. F.48: never return std::move(local), it blocks copy elision.
license_if_known: Standard C++ Foundation license (personal/internal business use)

recipe: F.16: cheap-to-copy in-parameters by value, everything else by const reference. F.20: return values, not out-parameters. F.21: return a struct for multiple outputs.
license_if_known: Standard C++ Foundation license (personal/internal business use)

recipe: Per.11 and F.4: move computation from run time to compile time. constexpr initialization removes both the runtime call and the static-init data race. You cannot race on a constant.
license_if_known: Standard C++ Foundation license (personal/internal business use)

recipe: Per.7, design to enable optimization: qsort throws away the element type and forces an indirect call per compare; a template sort keeps the type and inlines the comparison.
license_if_known: Standard C++ Foundation license (personal/internal business use)

recipe: Complex constructors and virtuals mean unmanaged reads, unmanaged icache, and unnecessary destructor writes. Acton's rule: the best code is code that does not need to exist.
source_name: Mike Acton, Data-Oriented Design and C++, CppCon 2014 slides
trigger_condition: Does the code use complex constructors?
_note: generic aphorism ('the best code is code that does not need to exist'); nothing actionable
_review_reason: generic aphorism ('the best code is code that does not need to exist'); nothing actionable

recipe: SL.con.2: std::vector by default. SL.con.1: vector or array over a C array. ES.27: std::array on the stack. SL.str.2: string_view for non-owning reads.
source_name: C++ Core Guidelines, SL: The Standard Library
license_if_known: Standard C++ Foundation license (personal/internal business use)
trigger_condition: Does the code use C-style arrays?

recipe: Per.1, Per.3, Per.6: do not optimize without a reason, ignore code that is not performance critical, and never claim a speedup without a measurement.
license_if_known: Standard C++ Foundation license (personal/internal business use)
trigger_condition: Is the code performance critical?

recipe: Per.10: lean on the static type system; void* and byte-level manipulation blind the optimizer. Per.4 and Per.5: complicated or low-level code is not automatically faster than simple code.
license_if_known: Standard C++ Foundation license (personal/internal business use)
trigger_condition: Does the code use low-level pointer manipulation?

recipe: Acton's rule of thumb: where there is one, there are many. Design the loop over the array first, the single object second. Look on the time axis too.
source_name: Mike Acton, Data-Oriented Design and C++, CppCon 2014 slides
trigger_condition: Does the problem involve one object that may become many?

recipe: Struct with padding, or a loop touching one field: std.MultiArrayList keeps a separate array per field. Get the pointers once with slice(), then .items(.field) inside the loop.
trigger_condition: Does the loop touch only one field of a struct?

recipe: MultiArrayList also splits a tagged union into .tags and .data arrays. Scan tags alone without dragging payloads through the cache. Untagged unions are rejected.
trigger_condition: Does the code scan tags of a tagged union?

recipe: extern struct for C ABI layout. packed struct is a backing integer with bit-level fields, no padding, @bitCast-able. Plain struct layout is unspecified, which is what lets the compiler pack it.
trigger_condition: Does the struct need C ABI layout?

recipe: Alignment is always a power of two below 1<<29. Over-aligned pointers coerce down, never up. @alignCast when you know better than the type, and it is safety-checked.
trigger_condition: Does the pointer alignment differ from the type's alignment?

recipe: CLI run, frame loop, or request handler: ArenaAllocator over page_allocator, defer arena.deinit(), free nothing individually. Freeing a non-most-recent allocation inside an arena is a no-op anyway.
source_name: Zig Language Reference, Choosing an Allocator
trigger_condition: Does the code allocate many objects per operation?

recipe: Upper bound known at comptime: std.heap.FixedBufferAllocator over a stack buffer, zero heap traffic. Layer it under an arena when the cycle has a known cap.
source_name: Zig Language Reference, Choosing an Allocator
trigger_condition: Is the maximum allocation size known at compile time?

recipe: Library code takes an Allocator parameter and lets the caller pick. Do not bake in a global allocator; that decision belongs to the program, not the library.
source_name: Zig Language Reference, Choosing an Allocator
trigger_condition: Is the code a reusable library component?

recipe: Known append count: ensureTotalCapacity or ensureUnusedCapacity first, then appendAssumeCapacity. Growth is super-linear for amortized O(1), but every grow invalidates element pointers.
trigger_condition: Does the code keep element pointers across appends?

recipe: inline for unrolls at comptime. The langref says use it only when the semantics need comptime, or when a benchmark proves the unroll faster. Do not unroll on vibes.
trigger_condition: Does the code require comptime semantics?

recipe: Zig 0.14+: @branchHint(.cold) (replaces @setCold) must be the first statement of the unlikely branch or function. @prefetch for predictable non-sequential loads: no semantic effect, and a no-op if the CPU lacks the instruction.
_original_recipe: @branchHint(.cold) as the first statement of the unlikely branch or function. @prefetch for predictable non-sequential loads: no semantic effect, and a no-op if the CPU lacks the instruction.

recipe: Zig @Vector(N, T) is element-wise SIMD over bools, ints, floats and pointers. @splat widens a scalar, @reduce collapses, @shuffle and @select rearrange. Any comptime length works; small powers of two are typical, and lengths past native SIMD width split into several instructions.
_original_recipe: @Vector(N, T) is element-wise SIMD over ints, floats, bools, pointers. @splat to widen a scalar, @reduce to collapse, @shuffle and @select to rearrange. Small powers of two, 2 to 64.
_review_reason: langref allows any comptime length up to 2^32-1; 2-64 is only 'most typical'

recipe: comptime is the fast path for generics: comptime T: type is compile-time duck typing, monomorphized, no vtable. Types are first-class but only inside comptime-known expressions.
Zig has a noalias keyword, but the language reference still says TODO add documentation for noalias. Do not build an optimization argument on it yet.

Zig master build modes are -Doptimize=debug/safe/fast/small (0.15 and earlier: Debug/ReleaseSafe/ReleaseFast/ReleaseSmall). fast turns safety checks off; safe keeps them at medium speed. Benchmark safe first; a debug build is not a performance data point.
_original_recipe: -Doptimize=fast means optimizations on and safety off; safe keeps the checks at medium runtime speed. Benchmark ReleaseSafe first. A debug build is not a performance data point.
_review_reason: version-sensitive: -Doptimize=fast/safe is Zig master naming; 0.15 and earlier use ReleaseFast/ReleaseSafe

recipe: -fsingle-threaded demotes thread-locals to plain globals and drops the sync overhead. Free win for a genuinely single-threaded program.
source_name: Zig Language Reference, Single Threaded Builds
trigger_condition: Is the program single-threaded?

recipe: Zig style: no Value, Data, Context, Manager, State, utils, misc, or initials in type names. Everything is a value. Avoid redundant segments in fully-qualified names.
trigger_condition: Do type names use a single concrete noun?
